title: Cerebral babesiosis
definition: Acute cerebral signs (marked change in behaviour, stupor, semi-coma, coma or seizures) in a dog with a Babesia-positive blood smear and a normal or raised blood glucose [R1]. At post mortem the hallmark is microvascular brain injury with haemorrhage [R1][R2].
definition_note: Working definition confirmed and narrowed. The Onderstepoort B. rossi definition requires a normal or raised blood glucose, because hypoglycaemia causes the same signs [R1][R3]. Indian B. gibsoni studies used a different definition: neurological signs plus parasites in red cells of cerebrospinal fluid [R4]. Ataxia alone is not enough: cerebellar ataxia is reported as a separate, milder complication [R5].
key_points: Measure blood glucose first in every babesiosis dog with seizures, stupor or coma: hypoglycaemia gives the same signs and many past cases of cerebral babesiosis were probably hypoglycaemia [R3].
True cerebral babesiosis is rare (6 of 320 B. rossi dogs) but nearly always fatal (6 of 6 died or were euthanased) [R1].
Diminazene overdose or a repeated dose can cause central nervous toxicity with brain haemorrhage that mimics cerebral babesiosis: check the drug history [R6].
No treatment aimed at the brain lesion has been tested in dogs with babesiosis. Seizure control and raised intracranial pressure are treated as for any cause (level D) [R7][R8].
In an unvaccinated dog with neurological signs, keep rabies on the list even when the smear is positive [R9].

description.heading: What it is
description.text: A hyperacute neurological form of complicated babesiosis, with rapid progression [R6]. Clinically it is defined by cerebral signs with a positive smear once hypoglycaemia is excluded [R1]. Pathologists define it by lesions in the brain; clinicians in a living dog cannot see these, so the clinical diagnosis is less certain [R1].

description.heading: How common, and in which dogs
description.text: In 320 PCR-confirmed B. rossi dogs at Onderstepoort it occurred in 6 (1.3%), and these were 16% of all deaths [R1]. In 63 Hungarian B. canis dogs it was 3% [R10]. In an Indian B. gibsoni cohort 11 of 136 smear-positive dogs (8.1%) were classed as cerebral, but these dogs were selected for signs [R11]. South African practitioners listed it among the most common complicated forms in a 1993 survey [R12].

description.heading: When in the course of disease
description.text: Signs are usually present at admission and progress within hours; one dog became tetraplegic within hours of hind-limb ataxia [R6]. In a Brazilian necropsy series, four of seven dogs died suddenly within about 24 hours [R13]. Delayed cerebellar signs 9 days after uncomplicated disease were reported in one South African dog [R5].

description.heading: Mechanism
description.text: In 50 brains from natural cases (Onderstepoort group), the first lesion was focal endothelial injury and necrosis, with parasitised red cells packed in, and adhering to, capillaries. Lesions progressed to perivascular haemorrhage and then haemorrhagic infarction [R2]. Similar congestion, oedema and sequestration were found in B. canis [R14] and B. gibsoni [R4] cases. A raised serum manganese was found in 7 B. canis dogs with cerebral signs; its role is unknown [R15].

species_notes.note: The main South African evidence: 6 of 320 cases, all died [R1]; CNS involvement carried a 57-fold greater chance of death in 56 complicated cases [R16]; 50 brains described at post mortem [R2].

Case reports and small series from Europe: one Belgian dog recovered fully after imidocarb [R17]; one French dog died 6 h after admission with ARDS [R18]; brain oedema was found in all 6 fatal Polish cases, but only one had seizures [R14].
One Indian cohort (11 dogs, CSF-positive) is the only treatment follow-up: 9 of 11 dead by day 28 on diminazene-based treatment [R4].

criteria.criterion: Acute cerebral signs with a positive blood smear
criteria.threshold: Stupor, semi-coma, coma, seizures or marked behaviour change
Normal or raised; hypoglycaemia below 3.3 mmol/L
criteria.note: Leisewitz used below 3.3 mmol/L [R1]. Keller used below 3.3 mmol/L and called below 2.2 mmol/L severe (converted from the source units) [R3].

criteria.criterion: Parasites in red cells of cerebrospinal fluid, or B. gibsoni DNA in CSF
criteria.note: Used in one Indian B. gibsoni cohort only [R4][R11]. Blood contamination of the sample was not excluded; the definition is not validated.

clinical_signs.note: Core signs of the B. rossi definition [R1]. Seizures in 6 of 11 B. gibsoni dogs [R4].
Ataxia in 8 of 11 and paraplegia in 2 of 11 B. gibsoni dogs [R4]. Rapid progression to tetraplegia is reported [R6].

clinical_signs.sign: Paddling, opisthotonus, decerebrate or decerebellate rigidity
clinical_signs.note: Each in 4 to 7 of 11 B. gibsoni dogs [R4].
Listed in reviews and series [R6][R4]; vocalisation in 3 of 7 Brazilian necropsy cases [R13].

clinical_signs.sign: Cerebellar ataxia without other cerebral signs
clinical_signs.note: Two case reports, both improved; may be a separate, milder complication [R5].

tests.finding: Hypoglycaemia explains the signs; normal or high glucose is needed for the diagnosis
tests.note: Mandatory in collapsed dogs, puppies, and dogs with severe anaemia, vomiting or icterus [R3].

tests.finding: Confirms babesiosis; anaemia may be mild in cerebral cases
tests.note: Mean haemoglobin was 102 g/L at admission in 11 B. gibsoni cerebral dogs [R4].

tests.finding: Look for other organ failure and for metabolic encephalopathies
tests.note: Each was associated with death in B. rossi [R1].

tests.finding: Records depth of coma and change over time
tests.note: Validated in head trauma, not babesiosis: a score of 8 gave about 50% survival at 48 h [R19].

tests.finding: Parasitised red cells or B. gibsoni DNA
tests.note: Referral; one cohort only, method not validated [R4][R11].

tests.finding: Focal CNS lesions with rim enhancement in severe B. canis
tests.note: Referral; one experimental contrast study, number of dogs not given [R20].

tests.finding: Swelling, congestion, petechial haemorrhage, white-matter malacia, oedema
tests.note: Gross lesions in 31 of 50 brains; oedema in 18 [R2].

differentials.distinguish: Glucose below 3.3 mmol/L; signs respond to dextrose. Found in 19% of B. rossi dogs and linked to collapse and young age [R1][R3]. See SY16.

History of overdose or repeated doses; post mortem cortical haemorrhage and oedema look like cerebral babesiosis [R6]. Transient neurological signs 3 days after diminazene were reported in a pup [R21].
Unknown vaccination status and no response to treatment; one B. canis dog thought to have cerebral babesiosis had rabies at post mortem [R9].

differentials.condition: Distemper, trauma, idiopathic epilepsy, uraemic encephalopathy
differentials.distinguish: These were exclusion criteria in the Indian B. gibsoni cohort, which also required full vaccination [R11].

differentials.condition: Hepatic or uraemic encephalopathy in complicated babesiosis
differentials.distinguish: Measure bilirubin, urea and creatinine; these rise with severity in B. rossi [R1]. No study compared them with cerebral cases.

approach.detail: Do it before anything else in a dog with seizures, stupor or coma [R3]. If below 3.3 mmol/L, treat hypoglycaemia (see SY16) and reassess [R1].
A seizure over 5 minutes is status epilepticus. Give a benzodiazepine first; intranasal midazolam works without IV access [R7][R22].
Oxygen, IV fluids and transfusion were part of care in the reported series [R14][R1]. Treat the anaemia (SY01) and shock (SY10).

approach.action: Give the antibabesial drug, and check the drug history
approach.detail: See TX00. Ask how much diminazene was given and when: overdose or repeat dosing can cause CNS toxicity [R6]. After 4.2 mg/kg IM, Miller advised no repeat within 21 days [R23].
Phenobarbital or levetiracetam [R7]. Reduce levetiracetam in kidney injury [R24].
Unknown or absent vaccination, or no response to treatment [R9].
For coma, falling coma score, suspected raised intracranial pressure, CSF or MRI [R19][R8].
Mortality in B. rossi was 6 of 6, including euthanasia [R1].

treatments.name: Intravenous dextrose for hypoglycaemia
treatments.aim: Correct hypoglycaemia, the most common mimic of cerebral babesiosis.
treatments.evidence_summary: Keller recommends glucose measurement in at-risk babesiosis dogs and says hypoglycaemia should be suspected in any comatose dog [R3]. No babesiosis study gives a dextrose dose. The dose below is from one non-babesiosis case report (insulin overdose) [R25]. More detail is on SY16.

doses.frequency: repeated whenever glucose was below 3.3 mmol/L, until 5.0 mmol/L or more
doses.context: One dog, insulin overdose, case report (not babesiosis)
doses.note: The same dog also received 5% dextrose at 2.5 mL/kg/h.

treatments.cautions: Recheck glucose after each bolus; refractory hypoglycaemia needed a glucagon infusion in the case report [R25].

treatments.name: Benzodiazepines (midazolam, diazepam) for seizures
treatments.aim: Stop status epilepticus or cluster seizures.
treatments.evidence_summary: First-line drugs in the ACVIM consensus for dogs with any cause of status epilepticus [R7]. In a trial of 35 dogs with epilepsy, intranasal midazolam stopped status epilepticus in 70% and rectal diazepam in 20% [R22]. Not studied in babesiosis; diazepam was used in one fatal B. canis case [R14].

doses.frequency: bolus; repeat or start an infusion because the half-life is about 1 h

doses.note: If boluses fail, an infusion of 0.1 to 0.5 mg/kg/h or another drug.
Less effective than intranasal midazolam in this trial.

treatments.cautions: Repeated diazepam boluses accumulate and can cause severe CNS depression and cardiorespiratory collapse; the propylene glycol vehicle can cause phlebitis and hypotension [R26]. All trial dogs were sedated and ataxic [R22].
treatments.monitoring: Seizure activity, respiration, mentation, blood pressure.

treatments.name: Phenobarbital
treatments.aim: Second-line control of seizures that recur after benzodiazepines.
treatments.evidence_summary: Second-line drug in the ACVIM consensus for seizure emergencies of any cause [R7]; doses from the IVETF epilepsy consensus [R24]. Not studied in babesiosis.

doses.frequency: divided into doses of 3 to 5 mg/kg
then two boluses of 4 to 6 mg/kg, 20 min apart
doses.context: Rapid loading used by some authors, IVETF consensus

treatments.cautions: Sedation and ataxia are common; hepatotoxicity is an uncommon idiosyncratic effect [R24]. Use with care in dogs with babesial hepatopathy (SY06).
treatments.monitoring: Mentation and respiration during loading; serum concentration 14 days after starting [R24].

treatments.name: Levetiracetam
treatments.aim: Second-line seizure control with little liver metabolism.
treatments.evidence_summary: Second-line drug in the ACVIM consensus [R7]. In a placebo-controlled trial of 19 dogs with status epilepticus or repetitive seizures, 56% responded to IV levetiracetam and 10% to placebo, with no serious adverse effects [R27]. Not studied in babesiosis.

doses.frequency: once after a seizure, then 20 mg/kg every 8 h

treatments.cautions: Consider a lower dose in impaired renal function [R24]; kidney injury is common in complicated babesiosis (SY05).

treatments.name: Mannitol
treatments.aim: Lower raised intracranial pressure from brain oedema.
treatments.evidence_summary: Given to one B. canis dog with seizures that died; brain oedema was found in all 6 fatal cases of that series [R14]. No babesiosis study measured an effect. The dose is from a study of 13 dogs with intracranial hypertension of other causes (level D for the dose) [R8].

doses.context: 13 dogs with suspected intracranial hypertension, other causes

treatments.cautions: Give only to euvolaemic, well-hydrated dogs, because of diuresis and hypovolaemia; use with caution in hypovolaemia [R8]. Many babesiosis dogs are hypotensive or have kidney injury (SY10, SY05).
treatments.monitoring: Electrolytes, hydration, urine output, blood pressure [R8].

treatments.name: Hypertonic saline
treatments.aim: Lower raised intracranial pressure with less diuresis than mannitol.
treatments.evidence_summary: No use in babesiosis was found. Studied in 15 dogs with intracranial hypertension of other causes [R8].

doses.context: 15 dogs with suspected intracranial hypertension, other causes

treatments.cautions: Sodium and chloride stayed raised and potassium fell after the bolus [R8].

treatments.name: Glucocorticoids
treatments.evidence_summary: One dog with delayed cerebellar ataxia, blindness and quadriparesis improved on prednisolone [R5]. Dexamethasone was part of care in fatal B. canis cases [R14]. In a 1993 South African survey, most practices gave supportive corticosteroids to all babesiosis cases [R12]. No controlled study; no source read gave a dose for this use.
treatments.cautions: No safety data for this use in babesiosis were found.

treatments.name: Oxygen and nursing of the recumbent dog
treatments.aim: Prevent hypoxia and complications of recumbency.
treatments.evidence_summary: Oxygen was part of care in fatal B. canis cases [R14]. Tissue hypoxia is thought to play a major role in severe B. rossi disease [R28]. No study tested oxygen or nursing in cerebral babesiosis. Lung injury can occur with it (SY08) [R18].
treatments.monitoring: Respiratory rate and effort, pulse oximetry or blood gas, coma score [R19].

prognosis.text: Poor. All 6 B. rossi dogs with cerebral babesiosis died or were euthanased [R1], and CNS involvement carried a 57-fold greater chance of death [R16]. Mortality was described as almost 100% in a series of 50 brains [R2]. In B. gibsoni, 9 of 11 died by day 28 [R4]. Single B. canis and cerebellar cases improved, one with full neurological recovery [R17][R5].

indicators.finding: Cerebral signs with normal glucose (B. rossi)

indicators.meaning: Hypoglycaemia, not cerebral babesiosis; hypoglycaemia itself raised the odds of death 3.5-fold in B. rossi [R1].
Multiple organ involvement carried a poor prognosis in B. canis [R10]; renal involvement raised risk 5-fold in B. rossi [R16].

related.why: Antibabesial drugs, and diminazene dosing limits.
Hypoglycaemia, the first cause to rule out.
Triage and order of care in complicated disease.
Lung injury (ARDS) can occur with cerebral babesiosis.
Muscle tremor and pain from rhabdomyolysis.

evidence_gaps: No treatment trial in cerebral babesiosis of any species.
No study in B. rossi describes clinical signs, imaging or CSF in living dogs.
No study measured intracranial pressure, or tested anticonvulsants, mannitol, hypertonic saline or glucocorticoids, in dogs with babesiosis.
The CSF-based definition used for B. gibsoni has not been validated against blood contamination.
Whether survivors have lasting neurological deficits is not reported, apart from single case reports.
No source read gave a dextrose dose for babesiosis-associated hypoglycaemia.
A 2022 University of Pretoria dissertation on B. rossi cerebral histopathology (Lewis) has no abstract and was not read.

search.note: Searched cerebral babesiosis, neurological signs, diminazene toxicity and the candidate treatments, plus status epilepticus and intracranial hypertension guidance in dogs. Several older South African papers (1947 to 1981, including diamidine poisoning) have no abstract online and were not used; most Indian and Brazilian reports are low quality.
